title: Pam East Designs: A career 26 years in the making gets a life-changing boost from Photoroom
summary: Learn how this world-renowned jewelry maker and teacher has used Photoroom to launch her seasoned business into a new era of success.
body_text: The challenge: Pam East faced a significant challenge in modernizing her long-standing business while maintaining the high-quality imagery required for her handmade silver jewelry. With marketing demands and platforms constantly changing and shifting, Pam needed a quick and effective way to create professional-looking product photos for her Etsy store and her jewelry-making classes without an extensive learning curve. Our solution: Photoroom proved to be a game-changer for Pam. The app’s user-friendly interface allowed her to produce high-quality images quickly. Features like AI Shadows , reflections, and AI photo editing tools enabled her to create stunning visuals that highlighted her jewelry pieces beautifully. Additionally, the ability to switch seamlessly between devices made her workflow more efficient. Results: Since incorporating Photoroom into her process, Pam has seen a substantial increase in both sales and engagement across her platforms. Her Etsy store now performs exceptionally well, with more visibility and positive responses to her product images. Moreover, Photoroom has saved her significant time (what took three days now takes three hours and what took weeks now takes days), allowing her to focus more on creating and teaching. Her classes have received great feedback, especially those that incorporate Photoroom, helping her students enhance their own photography skills and craft their own success. Pam East of Pam East Designs started making handmade silver jewelry in 1997. First promoting and selling her masterpieces at small craft shows, Pam—the 2024 Lis-el Crowley Vision Award winner —eventually moved to galleries and then her true passion, teaching jewelry making. Today, she sells her jewelry on Etsy and her jewelry-making classes on CraftCast . She also enjoys a large following on YouTube where she shares a variety of content on her jewelry-making processes and techniques. Based in Atlanta, Georgia for the majority of her career, today Pam is based in Olympia, Washington, but continues to travel the country and the world sharing her passion for beautiful jewelry and empowering others to create and succeed in their own right. Pam’s journey as a crafter began attending local craft fairs and over the years, her business grew significantly. From 2000 until the U.S. economic downturn of 2008—after a career-boosting appearance on the then wildly popular craft show The Carol Duvall Show —she also ran a successful enamel bead-making tools and supply business. Since then, Pam has focused more on teaching both in person and online through her captivating videos (her first one was on VHS tape!) and books. Since closing down the supplies business, Pam has continued to make strides in the jewelry-making and teaching space as a one-woman operation. This has meant wearing at least a dozen different hats at the same time, with the biggest one always being marketing. “Anytime you own your own business, I would say that 90% of your job is marketing and getting the word out. And it's changed so much in 26 years.” - Pam East, Founder, Pam East Designs In the past, marketing for Pam involved mostly writing for craft magazines (these were huge in the 90s and early 2000s) like Art Jewelry Magazine , Lapidary Journal , and Jewelry Artists , but now, it's all about the internet and streaming. And with new platforms like TikTok and YouTube shorts and reels becoming more and more influential, staying current and relevant is a constant and vigorous effort. But despite how much things have changed and continue to evolve over the course of her impressive 26-year career, Pam has been able to accomplish what many can’t. By staying curious and open to learning and adapting as many times as necessary, Pam East Designs has transcended industry trends and continued to bring inspiration and innovation to jewelry enthusiasts and makers around the world. And in the last year, Photoroom has been a game-changer for Pam’s business, giving her a huge amount of time back to focus more on creating and teaching, while still producing high-quality product photography and marketing to keep her business flourishing. Launching a seasoned business into a new era of success While preparing a new class for CraftCast titled, “ Phone Photography Secrets Revealed ,” Pam was trying to help her jeweler students take better pictures of their work, so she began searching for a good mobile photo editing tool. Essentially, Pam wanted to put a whole studio in a phone. “I had produced a class in 2017 using a DSLR camera but everybody now wants to use their phone for everything. So I thought, OK, phones have gotten good enough now where you can actually take really good pictures with them. Let me do a class on cellphone photography.” After looking at a bunch of different tools like Lightroom and Canva, Pam eventually stumbled upon Photoroom. She was immediately hooked by how user-friendly the tool was and how instant the results were. “The other platforms might have been able to do most of the things Photoroom does, but there was a big learning curve. I looked at Photoroom and there was no learning curve, just punch and play. I was up and running so fast. And I went, ‘I have to show this to my students!" Pam taught her class, half of which covered how to get a good photo to begin with. The other half dove into how to use Photoroom to edit that photo and take it to the next level. And everyone loved it. “Everybody was shocked at how much they could do with Photoroom right from their phone. They kept saying how life-changing it was. People are not generally photographers. They don’t have the background and they find it all so intimidating. But Photoroom changes that.” After that initial class, Pam got so much interest that she created an entire class on Photoroom —a deep dive on the platform including how to make your own backgrounds with AI ; how to insert backgrounds so that you can use the same one over and over again; how to use stickers and other fun elements—the whole nine yards. The class was so much fun and everyone loved it. Some students did complain that Photoroom isn’t free, but I explained it costs money because it’s worth something. If I want to hire a photographer to take one professional photo of one of my pieces, that’s going to cost more than the annual fee for Photoroom. And I am getting top-notch professional results with Photoroom.” - Pam East, Founder, Pam East Designs “So my introduction to Photoroom was wanting this studio-in-a-box. I have to say that now, I probably do half my work on my phone and half my work on the desktop. And that’s another thing I LOVE about Photoroom; that I can glide so easily back and forth from devices—whether I’m on my tablet, phone, or my desktop—all my media is right there.” Pam's favorite Photoroom features give her jewelry-making and teaching business a competitive edge Photoroom has transformed the way Pam works with images. Her favorite features include AI shadows and reflections , which add a professional touch to her photos with very little time and effort. She loves having complete control over the shadows, whether it's making a piece look like it's hanging in the air or placed against a wall. And reflections create a striking, mirror-like effect that enhances the presentation of her pieces. The photo editing tools are also essential for correcting lighting and color issues. With just a few tweaks, Pam can brighten dark images, adjust contrast, and correct color tones to make her silver pieces look perfect. Plus, by creating her own backgrounds using AI Backgrounds , Pam is able to keep her Etsy shop vibrant by matching backgrounds to the jewelry pieces—something she’s noticed really helps her break through the noise and stand out amongst other merchants. She also uses templates to streamline this process, allowing for quick adjustments and consistency across her photos. In addition to product photography, Pam uses Photoroom heavily for her video class content including creating crisp, concise jewelry-making process and tool stills, titles, and thumbnails. Pam finds this clarity is also crucial for standing out in a crowded online space. But her favorite professional use for Photoroom is teaching her students how to use the app to elevate their photography. “It’s incredibly rewarding to see how much Photoroom helps them showcase their work beautifully. I love giving people the tools they need to be successful. And I’ve gotten more positive feedback on my classes that involve Photoroom than on any other ones I’ve ever taught.” - Pam East, Founder, Pam East Designs Photoroom isn’t just for Pam’s professional work either; it’s proved to be a fantastic tool for personal projects too. Recently, during long hospital visits with her dad, Pam kept herself occupied and her spirits up by creating 100s of holiday pet portraits for friends and family with Photoroom. More Photoroom, more sales, more engagement Photoroom has become an indispensable part of Pam’s workflow, enhancing the quality of her images and her brand with powerful, user-friendly tools while increasing her searches and sales on Etsy and boosting her engagement on Facebook , her #1 marketing channel. “The time Photoroom saves me is HUGE. What took forever in Photoshop now takes seconds in Photoroom. It's phenomenal and fun!” - Pam East, Founder, Pam East Designs With more time to focus on creating and teaching, Pam is most excited about all the new classes, projects, and jewelry-making template and stamp designs she has in the works. As she continues to build on an already fun, thriving, and timeless career in jewelry-making; teaching; and content creation, Photoroom has significantly freed up more of her time to do more of what she loves; to dive deeper into her classes and provide an even better experience to her beloved students. “If you’re considering Photoroom, I highly encourage you to try it. The learning curve is NOTHING, and the [instant] results are worth every penny. Plus, you can be up and running in seconds. Photoroom is an invaluable tool for anyone looking to improve their photo editing quickly and easily. It’s worth it. It’s worth it. It’s worth it!” - Pam East, Founder, Pam East Designs Try Photoroom yourself today . Available on Android , iOS , or the Web .

title: HR Pulse: Engineering Series Part II – From Spark to Skill: How Our Engineers Found Their Path
summary: Mentorship is a game-changer. Growth isn’t always linear—and that’s okay. Lifelong learning fuels innovation. Teamwork and support systems matter. Discomfort often leads to the biggest breakthroughs.
body_text: Asking the Real Question When we sat down with our engineers, we didn’t just ask for their job titles or LinkedIn timelines. We asked something deeper: “How did you get to where you are today? ” It’s a simple question on the surface, but the answers revealed rich, layered journeys—full of career pivots, moments of doubt, unexpected mentors, breakthroughs, and countless small decisions that shaped their paths. We wanted real stories—the ones that don’t fit neatly into a resume but define a career. Two Journeys, Two Perspectives Alia Shah - Weapons Software Engineer, CAE USA Alia Shah – Weapons Software Engineer, CAE USA Alia Shah’s journey into engineering began in childhood, shaped by her experiences wandering museum halls and tagging along with her father at NASA. Her curiosity wasn’t a fleeting spark—it was, as she puts it , “a perpetual flame.” She was always drawn to solving problems, though early on she imagined a future in medicine or biomedical engineering. Her direction shifted in college, where she discovered a deep interest in systems-based design and aerospace engineering. That passion led her to pursue a Bachelor of Science in Engineering (B.S.E.) in Aerospace Engineering, along with a Minor in Mathematics from Texas A&M University . During her time at university, teamwork played a pivotal role in shaping her skills and mindset. Her senior capstone project was a defining experience: “Working in a team where everyone puts 100% of themselves in every day… I could never forget that. ” It taught her that engineering is not just about technical knowledge — it’s about collaboration, communication, and consistency. After graduation, Alia joined CAE USA , where her first day was filled with nerves. “An industry-level application of what I’d learned in school was simply out of my scope,” she admits. But what helped her bridge the gap between theory and practice was mentorship. “I had wonderful mentors to guide me… I tried to find connections between what I learned and what I needed to work on.” She quickly realized that even with a strong academic background and prior industry experience, challenges were inevitable. “Hurdles occur regardless of the environment,” she says. “Taking a different approach to every problem and staying consistent helped me get through.” At CAE, Alia continues to rely on collaboration across adjacent teams to navigate the steep learning curve. She’s also learned to balance work, friends, family, and personal time—an ongoing challenge, but one she meets by showing up every day and embracing progress one step at a time. Mentorship remains a cornerstone of her growth. “Engineers all conduct tasks in different ways, and the way certain programs or codes are written is subjective. Having a mentor sped up my understanding. Without feedback, it’s impossible to know whether you’re growing or what you can do to improve.” Alia’s advice? “Embrace failure and get a good mentor.” Matthew Kolb - Interop Software Engineer, CAE USA Matthew Kolb – Interop Software Engineer, CAE USA Matthew Kolb’s journey into engineering began in an unexpected place: cheat codes. As a kid, he was fascinated by how Action Replay codes worked for Nintendo DS games. That early curiosity about how things functioned behind the scenes sparked a deeper interest in technology and problem-solving. When it came time for college, Matthew initially pursued astronomy—driven by a love of the stars and inspired by his uncle. But the reality of the coursework didn’t match his expectations. “I was struggling and not enjoying my classes… having everything planned out from the start of college just isn’t possible. Roadblocks and detours happen ,” he reflects. That detour led him to computer science. Though it wasn’t his first choice, it quickly became a passion. “I’m glad I committed to it, as I get to spend every day working on things that I enjoy,” says Matthew . He went on to earn a B.S. in Computer Science and a B.S. in Mathematics from Central Michigan University . During college, Matthew acquired valuable experience working on a critical group project. He stepped up to support his peers, going above and beyond to help the team succeed. That moment solidified his understanding of collaboration and the importance of taking ownership—skills that would become central to his professional identity. Matthew’s first professional step into engineering came through a Co-op position at CAE USA . His first day was a whirlwind of nerves and orientation videos, but it quickly turned into a valuable learning experience. Early challenges taught him resourcefulness and persistence—traits essential for any engineer. As he transitioned into a full-time role at CAE, Matthew found his rhythm. He connected with his team, adapted to the work environment, and saw firsthand how collaboration accelerates growth. He credits his teammates as a major source of support during tough times and continues to prioritize teamwork and ownership in his role today. From cheat codes to software engineer Matthew’s journey shows that engineering paths aren’t always straight—but with curiosity, adaptability, and support, they lead to meaningful and rewarding careers. Matthew’s advice? “Don’t stress about not knowing something because everyone at some point had to learn these things.” Patterns, Surprises, and Lessons Learned What stands out in these stories isn’t just the technical milestones, it’s the habits and mindsets that made the difference: Mentorship matters. Both Alia and Matthew talk about the outsized impact of having someone to guide them, whether it’s a formal mentor or a supportive teammate. Learning never stops. Both Alia and Matthew talk about learning as a lifelong journey and sometimes it’s the hard problems, not easy ones, that refine your skills. Nonlinear paths are normal. Matthew’s switch from astronomy to computer science, Alia’s shift from biomedical interests to aerospace and then to guidance and control—these aren’t detours, they’re the journey. Teamwork and support systems. Capstone projects, teammates, loved ones—progress is rarely a solo act. Getting comfortable with discomfort. Both engineers describe nerves, self-doubt, and moments of feeling in over their head. Neither let those feelings stop them. What Can Aspiring Engineers Take Away? If you are early in your career or even just thinking about engineering, here’s what these stories offer: Don’t panic if your plan changes. Most people don’t have it all figured out from day one. Seek out mentors and support. The right guidance can make the hardest days manageable. Dive in, even if you’re nervous. The first day won’t be perfect, and that’s okay. Focus on what excites you. Passion for the work is what keeps you growing, learning and helps you face the most challenging times. Step up when the team needs you. You will learn the most when you take ownership of challenges. Nick Coucoules, Vice President, Airlift & Tankers, CAE USA Executive Perspective: Nick Coucoules on Building a Career with Purpose As we reflect on the diverse paths our engineers have taken, one message rings clear: growth is rarely linear, and success is built on a foundation of curiosity, resilience, and relationships. CAE Vice President of Airlift & Tankers and Tampa Site Manager, Nick Coucoules , embodies this truth. His journey is marked by pivotal moments, hands-on learning, and the guidance of mentors who helped shape his trajectory. Nick’s advice is both practical and relatable: never hesitate to ask for help and never stop learning. Whether you’re just starting out or leading a team, the best engineers—and professionals—are those who remain students of their craft. He also shares a powerful reminder: “How you do anything is how you do everything.” This principle transcends technical skill. It’s about how you show up—in interviews, solving complex problems, and everyday tasks. Your consistency, attention to detail, and integrity form the foundation of your personal brand. And in environments where people are always watching, these qualities matter. Nick encourages us to lead with confidence, stay grounded in humility, and always know our audience. When passion meets intentional action and self-awareness, you’re not just fulfilling a role, you’re shaping a meaningful career . Hear more from Nick: “One thing I love about working in the defense industry is its connection to the mission," Nick Coucoules, Vice President, CAE USA | LinkedIn The Road That Led Them Here So, how did our engineers actually get to where they are today? Through curiosity, grit, and a relentless drive to solve real-world problems. Their journeys are as diverse as the technologies they build—but each one is powered by a passion for learning and a commitment to making a difference. Whether they started in aerospace, software, or something entirely unexpected, they’ve all carved out paths defined by growth, collaboration, and innovation. A huge thank you to Alia, Matthew and Nick, and everyone else who shares their stories day after day. If you’re a CAE employee (or even just a reader with your own engineering journey), we’d love to hear your story or your questions—reach out and let’s keep the conversation going. Stay tuned to our next HR Pulse article , where we’ll dig into the tools and habits that help our engineers stay at the top of their game. Empower your future and transform your ideas into impactful solutions. If you are interested in a career at CAE USA, please visit our Careers website and connect with our team.

title: The practical value of long-range PCR for targeted HiFi sequencing
summary: Targeted workflow combines PCR-based enrichment with the accuracy, read length, and haplotype resolution of PacBio HiFi reads.
body_text: For clinical research laboratories evaluating long-read sequencing, the central question is often not whether longer reads are useful. The value is clearest in the places where conventional approaches have historically required a patchwork of assays: regions with high sequence similarity, repetitive elements, structural variation, repeat expansions, or haplotypes that cannot be resolved confidently from short fragments alone. That is where long-range PCR (LR-PCR) can play an important role. By amplifying larger DNA fragments, typically greater than 5 kb, LR-PCR gives researchers a way to focus sequencing on regions where completeness matters most. Instead of interrogating a complex locus through many short, overlapping reactions, labs can design either one or a small number of long amplicons that preserve the broader context of the region of interest. When those amplicons are sequenced with PacBio HiFi reads, the result is a targeted workflow that combines the depth and efficiency of PCR-based enrichment with the accuracy, read length, and haplotype resolution of HiFi sequencing. For defined clinical research questions, that combination can make difficult loci more accessible without requiring teams to move immediately to whole genome sequencing for every application. Explore our targeted sequencing resources, including practical guidance on LR-PCR design and workflow development. Explore targeted resources Overcoming short-read limitations in complex loci Many clinically relevant genes are challenging because the variant of interest is not always a simple single-nucleotide change in an easy-to-map region. These complex regions may contain segmental duplications, pseudogenes, GC-rich sequence, mobile elements, repeat tracts, or structural changes that span beyond the length of conventional short-read fragments. In those settings, the technical problem is not just generating sequence. It is keeping enough genomic context together to understand what is actually present on each allele. Traditional Sanger sequencing can be useful for small, defined targets, but complex loci often require many overlapping primer pairs and manual reconstruction across the region. Short-read panels can scale efficiently, but they can also lose physical linkage across variants, creating ambiguity in phasing, breakpoint interpretation, or repeat characterization. LR-PCR paired with HiFi long-read sequencing changes that starting point. A well-designed long amplicon can span the region of interest so that SNVs, indels, structural changes, repeat sequences, and nearby variants are read in the same molecule. That physical linkage is especially valuable for clinical research teams asking whether variants occur on the same chromosome or opposite chromosomes, whether a repeat expansion is associated with a particular haplotype, or whether a structural change alters the broader architecture of a locus. Consolidating Sanger, MLPA, and repeat-primed PCR into a single workflow The operational case for LR-PCR is closely tied to consolidation. In many targeted workflows, different variant classes have historically required different methods: Sanger sequencing for sequence-level changes, MLPA or arrays for copy number, repeat-primed PCR or Southern blotting for repeat expansions, and statistical approaches for haplotyping. Each method can answer part of the question, but each also adds handoffs, interpretation steps, and opportunities for uncertainty. A targeted HiFi workflow built on LR-PCR offers a more integrated path. For a given locus, the same amplicon can provide full-length sequence, direct read-backed phasing, breakpoint-level context for structural variation, and sequence-level information across repetitive or low-complexity regions. While it does not make assay design automatic or eliminate the need for validation, it does give laboratories a practical way to ask more complete questions from a single targeted experiment. This is the same kind of implementation question many labs are asking as long-read sequencing moves from evidence generation into operational planning. Where does a targeted long-read assay fit within an existing menu? Which applications benefit from a focused LR-PCR approach, and which are better served by HiFi whole genome sequencing? How can teams reduce complexity without sacrificing analytical confidence? Long-range PCR primer design best practices for HiFi sequencing The value of LR-PCR depends heavily on what happens before the sample reaches the sequencer. Primer placement, template quality, polymerase choice, and cycling conditions all influence whether the final HiFi dataset reflects the intended biology appropriately and reproducibly. For clinical research laboratories, that makes assay design a critical planning step. Primer binding sites should be selected outside repetitive sequences and away from common or clinically relevant polymorphisms where possible. Forward and reverse primers should be closely matched in melting temperature, screened for hairpins and primer-dimers, and checked for genome-wide specificity. High-molecular-weight DNA input is important because a broken template cannot support long-range amplification across the full target. Polymerase selection is equally important. Long amplicons require high processivity and high fidelity, particularly when the amplified material will be used for variant analysis. Gradient PCR, gel confirmation of a single clean band, and careful quantification before library preparation are practical quality checkpoints that can reduce downstream ambiguity. For detailed guidance on primer design, polymerase selection, and workflow optimization, visit our targeted sequencing hub to download resources including our LR-PCR Application note. Explore targeted resources When to use LR-PCR for targeted sequencing Despite its advantages, LR-PCR is not the answer to every clinical research sequencing question. If the goal is to discover variation broadly across the genome, HiFi whole genome sequencing may be the better entry point. Or if the priority is native methylation detection for your targets, amplification-free workflows that preserve base modifications, like PureTarget , should be considered. But when the question is defined, the locus is difficult, and deep targeted interrogation is needed, LR-PCR can be a highly practical front end for HiFi sequencing. This makes it particularly relevant for teams evaluating targeted approaches in areas such as inherited disease, carrier screening, pharmacogenomics, and other research applications where specific genes are known to be challenging for conventional methods. In these contexts, the value of LR-PCR is not simply that it produces a longer amplicon. The value is that it enables a more complete, phased, and interpretable view of a region that may otherwise be fragmented across multiple tests. Building a clinical research LR-PCR workflow with HiFi sequencing As clinical research labs consider how to adopt long-read sequencing, the practical details matter. A successful LR-PCR workflow starts with clear target definition, thoughtful primer design, high-quality DNA, the right polymerase system, and up-front optimization. HiFi sequencing can then convert that focused amplicon strategy into highly accurate long-read data to support more comprehensive analysis of difficult loci. The new PacBio LR-PCR Application note walks through this workflow step by step, from selecting target boundaries and screening primer sites to choosing polymerases, optimizing thermal cycling, preparing libraries, and troubleshooting common amplification issues. For labs moving from the idea of targeted long-read sequencing to practical assay development, LR-PCR offers a clear path forward with HiFi reads in a single assay. title: One Agent Per Customer
summary: See how our Solutions Architect Ilja built one agent per customer using Airbyte Agents.
body_text: A typical morning in my life as a Solutions Architect used to be quite hectic. While I was pouring my first coffee, customer requests and escalations would pile up in real time, short and critical-sounding, all saying things needed to be taken care of immediately. I manage about 20 to 30 accounts, and the context about each customer is spread across Salesforce, email, Slack, Zendesk, GitHub, Gong, and other internal systems. So before responding or taking a call, half the battle was a marathon of opening tabs and gathering the information. One customer sent a Slack over the weekend: one of their data channels needed a quick configuration change before Monday reporting, and they flagged it as urgent. I almost missed it while skimming the dozens of messages that poured in that morning. And then it dawned on me. The part eating up my time was not the actions of thinking and resolving. It was reconstructing the context from various systems and keeping track of many channels at once. So I gave every account its own agent Instead of building another dashboard or another workflow to support the meticulous information gathering and stitching, I decided to give every customer their own dedicated agent. The agent never sleeps, watches the customer’s incoming channels, and keeps track of the current context scoped to that customer. The main difference here, though: the agent decides the next best step and performs the action, gated on a final review before the email or Slack message hits the customer’s inbox. The agent runs the extra mile and presents a set of ranked options, cutting down not just the time to research the solution but also thinking multiple steps ahead, similar to how my own thinking would work when I draft the technical account plan for the customer. One plan per customer, multiple options ranked on impact, reliability, and cost, all presented for review by the customer’s agent as soon as there is more context available. The next learning had to come fast. Agentic runtimes are nondeterministic and inherently unpredictable. When you point a long-running agent towards multiple production APIs and evergreen context, the number of possibilities to calculate the next move is of exponential nature, like in a chess game. My first naive approach was to build better prompts, stricter instructions, rules in capital letters that say “Do not ever send a Slack DM without asking me first.” Prompts got longer, rules became skills, and the next model generations became smarter, but none of it made the agent deterministic in production. It turned out to be impossible to prompt your way to reliability. So the next insight was to keep thinking separate from context. The agent loop is nondeterministic and applies intelligence. Everything else, like retrieving information, building the context, and combining different outputs to ground the model, those are deterministic actions: schedules, procedures, access, and approvals, which need to happen reliably, every single time, with the same outcome. The context layer The boring, but critical part first: data plumbing. The agent is only useful with the data and context it can access to ground the model in truth. That data lives, for my accounts, in six to seven distinct systems which don’t usually talk to each other. The Airbyte Agents platform provides one single access point through the agent connectors. It’s the same connector foundation that used to move data into warehouses; now it’s used by agents instead. The agent can access the data without accessing credentials, so the auth lives in the connector layer, where it should be. Every connector provides a typed set of tools exposing each system over MCP, and the agent talks to the CRM with the same standardized language as to the support case data or the data lake. That wiring makes the system boring, or more accurately, predictable, which is the target for production systems that need to be as unexciting as possible when it comes to reliability. The hidden cost behind dozens of MCPs, always wired up, comes to realization later. Each connector has a few tools, and the number of tools compounds quickly. I stopped managing tool selection manually somewhere north of thirty MCP servers, so loading a few hundred tool schemas into the context window became quite expensive. That’s where deferred tool loading came in handy. The agent is smart enough to fetch the full schema only when the tools are needed; otherwise the tool names are enough to keep a reference to the capabilities of the MCP connector. Large surface area, small working set. The Context Store My first versions kept context the dumb way. Every run re-read the same threads, the same tickets, the same call notes, straight from the source APIs. That works right up until it does not: context windows balloon, paginated list calls drag on, and rate limits stop being theoretical when twenty agents wake up in the same hour. Airbyte Agents solves this with the Context Store, a managed and searchable replica of the useful entities from every connected source. Instead of crawling the support desk ticket by ticket to answer "what is open for this account," the agent runs one structured search against the store, with filters, field selection, sorting, and pagination, translated from a plain-language ask. Fewer tokens, faster answers, and the source APIs stay unbothered. The read and write paths split automatically. Reads that can tolerate a slightly stale copy go to the store. Anything real-time, and every write, goes through the connector to the live API. The store is scoped to the organization, so an agent only ever searches data its own org owns. This is also the piece that makes one agent per customer honest: their context stays current not because the agents never sleep, but because the replica is maintained for them while they do. Skills Skills are how I claw determinism back from the model. A skill is a procedure in a Markdown file: a name, a description, trigger phrases, then numbered steps. My morning triage is one. It pulls every ticket that changed since the last successful run, cross-references the support desk against Slack and the engineering tracker, computes SLA state deterministically instead of trusting anyone's dashboard, and writes me a brief sorted by who, let’s just say, needs attention most urgently. The point is not that the steps are clever. The point is that they are the same steps, in the same order, with the same output shape, every single run. When I improve the procedure I edit the file, and every future run inherits the change. The behavior lives in git, not in my head. This mattered the week I was traveling and slammed: the briefs kept coming out identical, because nothing about them depended on me remembering anything. Loops Skills say what. Loops say when. A loop is a scheduled tick registered with the operating system scheduler. It wakes, does one unit of work, and goes back to sleep. No open session. No human present. The design detail that matters is that a tick runs in one of three modes, and the mode is a cost decision. A deterministic tick is pure shell and spends zero model tokens. An agentic tick invokes the model. The third mode is the one I use most: a gated tick, where a near-free shell check runs first and the model is invoked only if the check finds something. Most ticks find nothing and cost nothing. My busy accounts tick hourly through the workday, weekdays only. Quiet accounts get one tick a day, in the early afternoon, when my laptop is reliably open. That asymmetry is the entire affordability story. The model is the exception, not the rule, which is what lets the whole fleet fire all day without the bill becoming a second mortgage. Watchers Loops poll on a schedule. Watchers wait for an event, and the reason they exist is a weekend I am still slightly embarrassed about. I once left an agent looping to see whether a customer had replied on a thread. Every few minutes it woke, re-read the whole context, concluded nothing had changed, and went back to sleep. It did this for two days. I paid for a full model invocation, dozens of times, to learn "no news" over and over. A watcher is the grown-up version. It polls the API directly from a shell script, holds no model context, and burns nothing while idle. When the reply actually lands, it wakes the agent, which spends tokens exactly once, at the moment there is finally something to do. Right now watchers are sitting on a handful of customer threads and one email chain for me. Idle is free. You pay only for the event. The orchestrator One agent per customer still leaves jobs that span all of them, like the weekly sweep across the whole book of accounts. For those there is an orchestrator, and the important thing about it is that it is dumb on purpose. It does no reasoning of its own and spends no tokens. It fans the job out, one scoped child agent per account, each in its own isolated context, then collects the results. Isolation is the payoff I did not appreciate until it saved me. One child hit a permissions error mid-sweep and died. The other nineteen finished fine, and the report simply noted the gap. The old serial version of that job would have dragged one bloated context through every account and taken the failure down with it. The one rule: it drafts, I send Nothing customer-facing sends automatically. Not email, not Slack, not a support ticket reply. Every outbound thing the system produces becomes a draft, and then a small bot DMs me out of band so the ping reaches my phone even when no session is open. I read it, sometimes I edit it, and then I send it. Every time. The line I hold is reversibility. Reading is reversible, so the agent does it alone. Drafting is reversible, same. Sending is not, so a human owns it, with no exceptions for confidence. The nightmare this prevents is specific: a fluent, plausible, wrong message going to my biggest account at the worst possible moment. And the rule is enforced in the plumbing, not in the prompt. The send path does not exist without me. The shape, assembled One picture instead of a thousand words of narration: a deterministic control plane drives the agent runtime, the runtime reasons over a governed context layer, and every outbound action is forced through the human gate before it touches the outside world. Why this shape Ranked, because the three properties are not equal. Safe to trust comes first. Access is governed at the connector layer and nothing irreversible happens without me, and without that property none of the rest would be allowed anywhere near my customers. Cheap to leave on comes second, since always-on is only real if idle costs nothing. Reliability I rank last, oddly. Not because it does not matter, but because it falls out of the other two: when procedures, schedules, and approvals are deterministic and the context lives in a managed replica, a failure degrades into a slightly stale read instead of a lost signal. Build your own Nothing here is specific to solutions architecture. If your work is spread across many tools, and you can name the moment each week where the gathering eats the thinking, the pattern transfers. A governed context layer through Airbyte connectors, with the Context Store keeping reads cheap and searchable. Procedures as version-controlled skills. Loops with cheap gates, and watchers so waiting is free. An orchestrator when the work is parallel. A human gate, in the plumbing, on every irreversible action. The models will keep getting better without any effort from you. The architecture is the part you build, and it is the part that decides whether you have a production system or a demo. If you want to give an agent governed access to your own systems, that is what Airbyte Agents is for. Start with the context layer, give the agent something real to read, and keep a human on the send button. Ready to build context-aware AI on your own data? [Get started with Airbyte Agents.]

title: Strategic information management in the digital age
summary: Corporate information management has undergone a steady evolution over the past three decades. Organizations that have been quick to embrace new strategies and tools are surviving and thriving in continuously changing business landscapes. Those that have not embraced the value of information are going under and facing a crowded, competitive marketplace filled with companies looking to pounce on the first signs of weakness or opportunity.
body_text: Corporate information management has undergone a steady evolution over the past three decades. Organizations that have been quick to embrace new strategies and tools are surviving and thriving in continuously changing business landscapes. Those that have not embraced the value of information are going under and facing a crowded, competitive marketplace filled with companies looking to pounce on the first signs of weakness or opportunity. Digital information management had its origins in a vision of a “paperless office” in the 1990s, targeting business documents with the appearance of the first built-for-purpose document management systems. It soon became clear that the true value of these systems was not merely in the freeing up of paper-based storage, but was actually in freeing up the inherent value in the documents, allowing access and retrieval of the right information, at the right time, by the right people. This provided immediate competitive advantage to the organization, as decision cycle time and reliability of the information underlying the decision were significantly improved. With the dawn of the new millennium, the bursting of the dotcom bubble ushered in a new era of corporate responsibility, and the recognition that a new layer of information management was needed. The value of information resources decayed over time and, indeed, as new legislation caught up with digital reality, it was recognized that some information could acquire negative value. Document management platforms evolved to add records management capability, allowing effective disposition or repurposing of information that no longer had original corporate value. In parallel, the importance of metadata tagging and classification to provide a different facet of information access became more and more apparent. Security tagging of these electronic resources addressed both protection of corporate intellectual property as well as client and customer data. By the middle 2000s, it was recognized that this tagging allowed both physical (e.g., models, prototypes, evidence boxes, etc.) and electronic information sources to be managed from a single platform, and the concept of enterprise content management was firmly established. However, this focus had been on unstructured information—the documents, faxes and letters (electronic or otherwise) that had brought the most tangible advantage in enabling access. The next step was to integrate this unstructured information with the traditionally more accessible structured information sources, such as ERP systems , to provide a 360-degree view of all relevant information (e.g., contracts, emails, correspondence, etc.), in the context of a structured business transaction. Examples are making decisions regarding, or engaging with, an employee, supplier or customer. This functionality was combined with high performance enterprise search capabilities, allowing searching across disparate enterprise silos and media, often including digital assets such as video. This strategy enabled enterprise information management , and from here it was a fairly small step to integrate this information flow with business process management , enabling a degree of tactical agility to give competitive advantage to the organization. However, we are now on the cusp of the true digital age. The market landscape in which the enterprise operates has changed beyond all recognition in the last five, let alone 30 years, and the pace of this change will only continue to accelerate, driven by social media, extreme connectivity and the expectations of a digitally-enabled millennial generation. To date, enterprise information management strategies have been inward-looking , but this is no longer sufficient. Just as enterprise information management brought competitive advantage by bringing together structured and unstructured content and process within the organization, strategic information management in the digital age will bring together internal intellectual property and close-to-real-time external market information for competitive advantage. The fundamental difference between this internal and external data is in the rate of decay of information value. The first organization to access, analyze and effectively action high-value external information will extract virtually all value from that external information, turning it into an internal corporate resource that will be the core driver behind both strategic and tactical decision in the enterprise. This will hold true whether the enterprise is operating in the cut-and-thrust of an existing market arena and needs immediate visibility of both threat and opportunity in this hyper-competitive “Red Ocean” environment, or needs to rapidly realign business strategy (or indeed adapt the existing business model) to exploit greenfield opportunities in the untainted “Blue Ocean”1 of potential presented by unexploited information deposits in this new gold rush. CGI is uniquely positioned to guide enterprises to tap this seam of opportunity. Over the past decades, we have provided organizations with a roadmap, tools and experience to maximize value from their information assets in the journey from document management to enterprise information management. Our strategic information management assessment package (SIMA) helps maximize the value of information from both inside and outside the organization to provide a strong competitive advantage. 1 INSEAD Professors W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne content in their 2005 book “Blue Ocean Strategy” that enterprise success can occur through creation of uncontested “Blue Ocean” market space rather than battling competition in the shark-infested “Red Ocean” of the competitive marketplace.

title: How to Add an AI Scribe to Jane App EHR in 2026
summary: Jane's native AI Scribe covers SOAP notes at low cost—but not claims across providers. See how a workforce platform handles multidisciplinary clinic billing.
body_text: You run on Jane App, the allied-health practice-management and EMR platform, whether you are a solo physiotherapist, chiropractor, or massage therapist, or a multidisciplinary clinic billing insurance across many provider types. Documentation weighs on all of it. Physicians spend close to two hours on the EHR and deskwork for every hour of direct patient care [1], and clinicians across settings log about 86 minutes of nightly "pajama time" finishing charts [2]. Here is the fact worth knowing up front: Jane already ships its own native AI Scribe. So the real decision is no longer whether to add a scribe. It is whether the native scribe covers everything you need, or whether clean claims across a multidisciplinary clinic and the other systems you run need more. This guide covers that honestly. Key Takeaway Jane App already has a native AI Scribe, built in-house to draft SOAP notes into the chart at low cost, so for allied-health documentation it covers a lot, especially for solo and small practices. Where it stops is clean claims across a multidisciplinary clinic and coverage across other systems. A clinical workforce platform adds that. Sully.ai integrates with Jane and adds an AI Coder that submits clean claims, plus intake and follow-up, across Jane and more than 20 other EHRs. What an AI Scribe Adds to the Jane App Workflow An AI scribe listens to the appointment and turns the conversation into a structured note. The practitioner stays present with the patient. The scribe drafts the note in seconds, and the practitioner reviews it instead of typing it. Jane's users span two kinds of work: cash-pay wellness like massage and some mental health, and insurance-billed care like physiotherapy and chiropractic. The numbers below are the burden a scribe is meant to remove. The difference on Jane is that a native AI Scribe already exists. So the decision shifts from "do we add a scribe" to "does the native scribe cover everything, or do clean claims across providers, and the other systems we run, need more." Ambient Documentation Versus Manual Charting The old flow is typing SOAP notes in Jane after each appointment. Either way the practitioner is still doing data entry. The ambient flow is listen, draft, review, sign, and ambient scribes have cut documentation time in multi-site studies [8]. The split that matters here is payer mix: massage and wellness are often cash-pay, while physiotherapy and chiropractic are insurance-billed and coding-sensitive, so on that side the note has to feed a clean claim. Jane Ships Its Own AI Scribe, So the Question Is Claims and Scale Jane offers a native AI Scribe, built in-house, that listens ambiently and drafts SOAP or progress notes into the chart. It is HIPAA and PIPEDA compliant and offered as a low-cost add-on at about $15 per practitioner per month with a free tier [3][4]. That is a strong allied-health-native tool, and Jane also owns scheduling, booking, and billing. So the decision is not native versus nothing. It is whether clean claims across a multidisciplinary clinic, and coverage across other systems, needs more than a documentation scribe is built for. That framing drives the rest of this guide. How AI Scribes Connect to Jane App There are three routes: Jane's native AI Scribe, a third-party scribe, or a clinical workforce platform. The depth decides how much of the work around the note a tool removes. The key distinction: documenting the visit and submitting insurance claims across a multidisciplinary clinic are different jobs, and a scribe only does the first. Integration type Documents the visit Beyond the note Insurance claims, across providers EHR reach Native (Jane AI Scribe) Yes, in-workflow Native scheduling and billing No claim submission Jane only Third-party scribe Yes None No Jane or many EHRs Clinical workforce platform Yes Claims, intake, follow-up Yes, submits claims Jane plus 20 more The Native Option, Jane AI Scribe Jane's own AI documents the visit with a scribe built in-house, listening ambiently and drafting SOAP notes into the Jane chart. It is HIPAA and PIPEDA compliant, low-cost, and saves 2 to 5 hours per week, and Jane also owns scheduling, booking, and billing [3][4]. This is a strong allied-health-native fit, with nothing to integrate. The honest limit is scope: the scribe documents, and it is not a coder that submits insurance claims across a multidisciplinary clinic. Third-Party Scribes Freed and S10.ai market AI scribes for Jane, and Upheal is a therapy-focused option often compared with Jane for mental-health practices [5][6][7]. These document well. The tradeoff is that they are documentation tools, and they stop at the note. Clinical Workforce Platforms The broadest tier. A clinical workforce platform integrates with Jane and adds agents across the visit and the work around it. Sully.ai integrates with Jane once, and then its agents share that connection: the AI Scribe documents, the AI Coder submits clean claims, the AI Receptionist supports scheduling and rebooking, and the AI Triage Nurse runs intake and follow-up. This is the option that adds claim submission across provider types and coverage across systems. How to Add an AI Scribe to Jane App Step by Step Five steps take you from decision to a validated note in the chart. 1. Confirm Your Jane Setup and Payer Mix Confirm your Jane setup, whether you have enabled the native AI Scribe, your disciplines, and your payer mix, cash-pay wellness versus insurance-billed physiotherapy and chiropractic. Decide what you want: SOAP documentation, which the native scribe may already cover, or clean claims across providers plus intake and follow-up, which points to a clinical workforce platform. That payer mix determines the route. 2. Choose Your Integration Method Map the methods to that goal. The native scribe gives you an in-workflow SOAP note. A third-party scribe documents. A clinical workforce platform handles documentation, clean claims, and intake through one integration. The decision rule: if you are a solo or small allied-health practice, the native AI Scribe gets you there. If you bill insurance across a multidisciplinary clinic or run more than one system, you need a clinical workforce platform. 3. Connect the Scribe For the native option, enable the AI Scribe in Jane [3]. For a third-party or workforce tool, have the vendor integrate with your Jane environment [5][6]. Whichever route you pick, two things are non-negotiable before any session audio is recorded: a signed BAA and HIPAA-compliant data handling, plus client consent for recording. 4. Map Notes and Coding to Jane Configure how SOAP notes land in the right Jane fields, and for physiotherapy and chiropractic how codes attach. The native scribe documents; a clinical workforce platform writes coded, claim-ready data and submits it. Verify it on an insurance-billed physio or chiro visit, not just a cash-pay wellness session, since that is where coding and claims actually matter. 5. Pilot Across Disciplines, Measure, and Scale Pilot across a cash-pay wellness session and an insurance-billed physio or chiro visit, since they end differently. The insurance visit is the one that reveals whether coding and claims hold up. Confirm notes land correctly, measure the time saved [3], and on the insurance side measure whether claims come out clean. Validate consent and governance before a clinic-wide rollout. What to Look For in a Jane App AI Scribe Four criteria separate the options on the shortlist. Allied-Health Fit Versus Claims Across Providers Jane's native AI Scribe is built for allied-health SOAP notes at low cost [3]. The question is whether you also need clean claims across a multidisciplinary clinic and intake and follow-up at scale, which the native scribe is not built for. Match the tool to your disciplines and payer mix, not just the single visit. Clean Claims for Physio and Chiro Physiotherapy and chiropractic are insurance-billed and coding-sensitive, and a multidisciplinary clinic bills across provider types. A scribe documents; submitting the claim is a separate job. This is where a busy clinic wins or loses revenue. Sully's AI Coder extracts every ICD-10 and CPT code and submits clean claims through one integration. Coverage Across Locations and Systems Multi-location and mixed clinics often run Jane plus other systems. Native tools cover only Jane. A workforce platform that integrates with Jane and more than 20 other EHRs covers them all through one approach. Weigh coverage against the systems you actually run. Security, Consent, and HIPAA Compliance The non-negotiables: HIPAA compliance , a signed BAA, encryption and de-identified PHI handling , MFA, SSO, role-based access, and clear retention controls. Add client consent for recording sessions. Ask where audio is processed, how long it is retained, and who can access transcripts before the pilot starts. Best AI Scribes for Jane App Five options worth shortlisting. Jane has a strong native AI Scribe, so it earns a place on the list, credited for what it does. 1. Sully.ai Sully.ai starts as a strong ambient scribe and extends into a coordinated AI workforce that integrates with Jane through a single integration. The AI Scribe documents the visit, then the AI Coder submits clean claims across provider types, the AI Receptionist supports scheduling and rebooking, and the AI Triage Nurse runs intake and follow-up. Against a low-cost allied-health-native scribe, the honest differentiators are specific. First, it submits clean claims across a multidisciplinary clinic, which a documentation scribe is not built to do, and where a busy clinic wins or loses revenue. Second, it adds intake and follow-up at scale, rebooking care plans and reactivation. Third, it covers Jane plus Epic, Cerner, Meditech, Athenahealth, and more than 20 other EHRs, which matters for multi-location groups, across 5,000+ providers and 50M+ hours of AI work delivered. Each AI role costs 80 to 90% less than the equivalent human role. Best fit: multidisciplinary and multi-location clinics on Jane that bill insurance or run more than one system. 2. Jane native AI Scribe Jane's own AI: a native ambient scribe built in-house that drafts SOAP notes into the chart, HIPAA and PIPEDA compliant and low-cost, alongside Jane's native scheduling, booking, and billing [3][4]. Standout: allied-health-native documentation at low cost with nothing to integrate. Best fit: solo and small practices that want fast SOAP notes inside Jane and do not need claim submission across providers. The honest limit is scope: it documents. 3. Freed A popular lightweight ambient scribe that markets an option for Jane and pushes chart-ready notes into the EHR [5]. Standout: clinician-loved and low-friction. Best fit: small practices that want a simple scribe, after confirming Jane fit. 4. S10.ai A cross-EHR ambient scribe that markets a progress-note taker for Jane [6]. Standout: broad EHR support. Best fit: practices wanting a cross-EHR scribe, after confirming Jane fit. 5. Upheal A therapy-focused AI EHR and scribe, often compared with Jane for mental-health practices [7]. Standout: behavioral-health depth. Best fit: therapy practices, after confirming Jane fit. Move From a Single Scribe to a Full AI Workforce Jane already documents the visit natively with its AI Scribe at low cost, which is genuinely strong for allied health. But a multidisciplinary clinic is a different scale of problem. A clinic bills insurance across physiotherapy, chiropractic, and more, and coding into a clean claim plus intake and follow-up is a different job a documentation scribe is not built for. The average hospital already runs on about 800 different software tools, and point-solution AI just adds more silos instead of a workforce. Sully takes the connected path. One integration with Jane, then a team of AI employees, the AI Scribe, the AI Coder, the AI Receptionist, and the AI Triage Nurse, sharing context across the visit. The Scribe writes the note, the AI Coder extracts every ICD-10 and CPT code and submits a clean claim across providers, and the AI Receptionist handles rebooking while the AI Triage Nurse runs intake, across Jane and any other system the clinic runs. Each AI role costs 80 to 90% less than the equivalent human role, proven across 5,000+ providers and 50M+ hours of AI work. If you are weighing an AI scribe for Jane, it is worth seeing what the full team looks like in action. FAQ Q: What is a Jane App AI scribe? A Jane App AI scribe is an ambient documentation tool that listens to the appointment and drafts a SOAP or progress note into the Jane chart, so the practitioner reviews and signs instead of typing. Jane offers a native AI Scribe, and platforms like Sully.ai integrate with Jane to add clean claim submission across provider types and intake and follow-up on top of documentation. Q: Does Jane App have its own AI scribe? Yes. Jane ships a native AI Scribe, built in-house, that drafts SOAP notes into the chart, HIPAA and PIPEDA compliant, as a low-cost add-on that saves 2 to 5 hours per week [3][4]. It documents allied-health visits well. It does not submit insurance claims across a multidisciplinary clinic or run intake at scale, which is where a clinical workforce platform adds value. Q: How do I add an AI scribe to Jane App? Decide whether the native scribe covers your needs or claims and scale need more. For SOAP documentation, enable the native AI Scribe [3]. For clean claims across providers and intake and follow-up, integrate a clinical workforce platform such as Sully.ai, confirm your Jane setup and payer mix, and pilot on an insurance-billed visit before scaling. Q: Does a Jane App AI scribe handle insurance claims and coding? Jane's native AI Scribe documents, and Jane has its own billing features, but the scribe is built for SOAP notes, not clean claim submission across a multidisciplinary clinic [3]. For physiotherapy and chiropractic billing across provider types, you need coding-to-claim, which a clinical workforce platform provides. Sully.ai's AI Coder extracts every ICD-10 and CPT code and submits clean claims through one integration with Jane. Q: Should we use the native Jane scribe or add a platform? Use the native AI Scribe if you are a solo or small allied-health practice that wants fast SOAP notes inside Jane at low cost [3]. Add a clinical workforce platform if you are a multidisciplinary clinic billing insurance or running more than one system. Sully.ai integrates with Jane and adds clean claims and intake across providers. summary: The Portland-Steamboat Springs route will operate Thursdays and Saturdays from Feb. 11, 2027, through March 28, 2027.
body_text: This winter, Alaska Airlines is launching new nonstop seasonal flights from Portland International Airport (PDX) to Yampa Valley Regional Airport (HDN), giving Oregon travelers an easier way to reach Steamboat Springs, Colorado, for skiing, hot springs and long-weekend winter getaways. GAAP total operating expenses of $66 million, compared to $89 million in the first quarter of 2025. title: Owning a Stock and Betting on One Are Two Different Things
summary: The return of single-stock futures reflects Wall Street's growing appetite for speculation. Know the difference between investing and wagering.
body_text: The return of single-stock futures reflects Wall Street's growing appetite for speculation. Know the difference between investing and wagering. KEY TAKEAWAYS Single-stock futures return after a previous eighteen-year experiment failed to attract meaningful trading volume. Lower margin requirements and a more leverage-friendly retail market have created a new opportunity for CME to try again. The contracts provide leveraged exposure to individual stocks without transferring ownership of the underlying shares. Investors receive cash gains or losses based solely on price movements. Single-stock futures differ significantly from options because losses are not capped and positions are marked to market daily. Overnight price moves can trigger margin calls and forced liquidations. Although the product has legitimate institutional hedging applications, the introduction of micro-sized contracts suggests retail participation is a primary growth target. The marketing reflects today's speculative trading culture. Investors should distinguish between owning a business and making a leveraged wager on its share price. Those are fundamentally different financial activities despite sharing the same ticker symbol. MY HOT TAKES Wall Street rarely abandons financial products forever; it simply waits for investor behavior to change before trying again. Today's return of single-stock futures reflects changing demand more than product innovation. Increased availability of leverage should not be confused with improved investment opportunities. Easier access often magnifies both gains and mistakes. Financial engineering continues to create more ways to speculate than to invest. The expanding menu of products makes investor education more important than ever. Marketing often emphasizes efficiency and flexibility while minimizing operational risks such as margin calls, overnight exposure, and liquidity. Reading the fine print matters more than ever. Long-term wealth creation still comes from owning productive businesses rather than continuously betting on short-term price movements. The distinction remains one of the most important lessons in investing. You can quote me: "Single-stock futures aren't making investing easier—they're making leverage easier." Anything goes. Wall Street has a habit of resurrecting things that already failed once, usually with better marketing the second time around. Today, CME Group is bringing back single-stock futures–a product so unloved the first time around that it quietly died in 2020 after eighteen years of nobody showing up. Now it's back, with lower margin requirements and a retail crowd that's spent the last few years getting very comfortable with leverage–perhaps a bit too comfortable. You may have noticed a growing number of ways for you to stake your money on what may be–in the future. Options, prediction markets, odd crypto tokens, complicated debt offerings. To be clear, all of these instruments are important with many specific uses, but investors need to understand the difference between owning any of these or the new, new futures, and owning a stock itself. Before you decide whether this belongs anywhere near your portfolio, let's talk about what it actually is. Let’s start with a little history lesson–you don’t have to take notes. Single-stock futures have a longer, weirder backstory than you'd guess for something debuting on your brokerage app today. Back in 1982, the SEC and the CFTC got into one of those turf wars only Washington could produce, and the compromise–the Shad-Johnson Accord–basically outlawed futures on individual stocks entirely. Nobody could trade them, for EIGHTEEN YEARS, because two regulators couldn't agree on who got to referee a product that didn't even exist yet. It took until 2000 for Congress to lift the ban, and by 2002 two exchanges rushed in to launch the product–OneChicago, backed by the CME, CBOE and CBOT, and a scrappier competitor called NQLX. NQLX folded by 2004, unable to find enough traders willing to show up. OneChicago hung around gamely for another sixteen years, even carving out a clever securities-lending niche nobody outside the industry ever heard of, and finally shut its doors in September 2020 having never built the volume its backers dreamed of. Two exchanges, two decades, one product Wall Street collectively shrugged at. That's the sequel nobody asked for, and yet here we are, watching the reboot–TODAY! So why bet on round two? Two things changed. First, after OneChicago closed, regulators quietly lowered the minimum margin requirement on these contracts from 20% of the position down to 15%–a little more leverage, a little more incentive for a trading desk to bother making markets in the product. Second, and more importantly, the retail appetite that OneChicago spent two decades waiting for actually showed up–it just showed up somewhere else. In case you haven’t noticed, options volume has exploded. Prediction markets went from a curiosity to a mainstream pastime. Crypto perpetual futures turned an entire generation of traders into people who think nothing of putting leveraged, single-name bets on with their thumb before finishing their coffee. CME isn't creating new demand for leveraged stock bets. It's just building a new pipe for demand that already exists. Here's what actually launches today, in plain English. CME is listing contracts on more than fifty of the largest U.S. stocks–names like Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla are all in the first batch. There are two sizes: a standard contract covering 100 shares of the underlying stock, and a "micro" version covering just 10 shares, aimed at smaller accounts. No stock ever actually changes hands. These are cash-settled, meaning the contract simply pays out the difference between where you entered and where the stock closes, in cash. And they trade on CME's Globex platform for nearly 23 hours a day, which sounds convenient until you think through what that actually means for risk management. More on that in a minute. The pitch is capital efficiency, and to be fair, it's a real pitch. Instead of paying full price for 100 shares of a stock, you put up roughly 15% of the contract's value as margin and control the full position. There's no borrowed-money interest ticking away in the background the way there is with a traditional margin loan against stock. You get outsized exposure for a fraction of the outlay. That's the appeal in a sentence, and it's also exactly why this thing requires some caution. There's also a legitimate use case buried under all the leverage talk, and it belongs to a different kind of investor than the one CME is really courting. A portfolio manager sitting on a concentrated stock position–say, an executive with a mountain of company shares who isn't allowed to sell–can use a single-stock future to hedge that exposure without disturbing the underlying shares or triggering the tax hit a sale would create. That's precision hedging, and it's genuinely useful. It's also almost certainly not why this product is launching with a "micro" contract sized for ten shares and marketing copy aimed squarely at the retail trader who's already comfortable dialing risk up on individual names through options. Institutions have had other ways to hedge concentrated positions for years. This launch is chasing a different crowd, and it's worth being honest with yourself about which one you are. Let's talk about how this differs from an option, because that's the comparison most of you will actually be making. When you buy a call or a put, your worst-case outcome is capped and known in advance: you can lose what you paid for it, the premium, and not one penny more. Full stop. That ceiling doesn't exist with a future. Buy a single-stock future and your gains and losses track the stock dollar-for-dollar on a leveraged base, in both directions, with no ceiling and no floor. There's also no time decay working against you the way an option slowly bleeds value as expiration approaches–which sounds like a benefit, and in a narrow sense it is, but it also means there's no clock running out the risk. Every overnight move hits the account directly, for as long as the position is open. There's also a tax wrinkle worth knowing before you assume this behaves like every other futures contract you've heard about. Most exchange-traded futures–the ones on the S&P 500, crude oil, gold–get a genuinely favorable tax treatment, a blended rate that treats 60% of gains as long-term and 40% as short-term no matter how briefly you actually held the position, plus a loss carryback other asset classes don't get. Single-stock futures were specifically carved OUT of that treatment when the rules were written decades ago. They're taxed the same plain-vanilla way a stock trade would be–ordinary short-term or long-term gains, depending on your holding period, nothing special about it. So if part of the pitch you hear is "it's a futures contract, it gets the good tax treatment"–that part doesn't apply here, and your accountant will not be impressed if you assumed otherwise. The product borrows the word "futures" and some of its mechanics, but not all of its perks, and the fine print matters more than the marketing. Now, the caution I promised you. Because these contracts mark to market daily, gains and losses settle into your account every single night, not just when you decide to close the trade. If a stock moves against you hard enough, your broker can issue a margin call, and if you don't meet it fast enough, the broker can liquidate the position without waiting around for a conversation, a phone call, or your permission. Combine that with nearly round-the-clock trading, and you've got a setup where an earnings surprise or a stray headline out of Washington can move a name while you're asleep, with no chance to react until you check your phone in the morning and the damage is already sitting in your account. That's a meaningfully different experience than owning the stock outright, where the worst that happens overnight is a bad number on a screen you can choose not to look at until you've had your coffee. And because this is a brand-new product reviving one that failed for lack of interest the first time around, there's no guarantee liquidity shows up cleanly out of the gate–early pricing on a new contract can be jumpy and spreads can be wider than advertised, until market makers find their footing and enough volume shows up to make prices behave. Which brings us back to where we started. The menu of ways to bet on where a number lands by a certain date keeps getting longer–options, prediction markets, crypto tokens, complicated debt structures, and now single-stock futures dusted off after a six-year nap. Anything goes these days, and increasingly, it does. But betting on a price and owning a business are not the same act, even when they're both denominated in the same ticker symbol. A share of stock is a claim on a company–its earnings, its dividends, its vote at the annual meeting. A single-stock future is a wager on where that stock's price sits on a specific date, nothing more. There's nothing wrong with placing that wager, plenty of professionals do it responsibly every day, hedging real exposure rather than gambling on it. Just make sure you know which one you're actually holding before you fund the account. FRIDAY’S MARKETS Stocks closed little changed on Friday, with the S&P 500 up 0.05%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 0.46% (235 points) to 51,947, and the Nasdaq Composite down 0.64%, weighed down by chip stocks. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.69%, retreating after briefly topping 4.7%--its highest level since January 2025 just the day before. WTI crude settled lower on the day, though reported closing prices vary by source. NEXT UP Durable Goods Orders (June) climbed by 0.3% missing estimates after sliding by -4.0% in May. Later this week aside from an FOMC meeting which will determine how relaxing your August is, we have a busy earnings week with a handful of mega cap techs amongst many others. Also, Consumer Confidence, more housing numbers, a first whack at Q2 GDP, Personal Income, Personal Spending, PCE Price Index, and University of Michigan Sentiment. You WILL check back often, if you want to avoid getting swept away in the current. 🏊 Important earnings today: Rambus, Welltower, Brown & Brown, Navitas Semiconductor, Universal Health Services, Nucor, Applied Digital, and Cadence Design Systems.
